rv.q: It’s a broken, brilliant Seagull – and it flies.
If you’re open to a show that makes noise quietly and thinks deeply, this ‘Seagull’ really flies.
The transfixing performance is by Indira Varma, who plays the star actress Arkadina with a sublime composure.
It’s an exciting break with tradition, converting its star power into a darker, weirder, and more satisfying kind of energy.

This long-awaited production follows a celebrated run of Lloyd’s fiercely modern, slam-poetry styled Cyrano de Bergerac, starring a swaggeringly seductive James McAvoy, which was similarly revived in spring 2022.
This is a maverick show that, like Oklahoma! at the Young Vic, proves how dangerous and daring a revival can be.
In abstract terms, the approach hangs together and yet, in contrast with Cyrano, it feels unsatisfying to watch, self-negating.
But this self-consciously languorous production is going to be divisive.
Yes, you feel trapped, suffocated by Lloyd’s pretentiousness.

Lloyd’s The Seagull is a most unusual interpretation, but it works, making the play feel more relevant than I can remember from previous productions as well as making each member of the audience feel that the cast is performing it, especially for them.
Reiss’s telling hits the human spirit with great exactitude.
The phenomenal acting performances of this universally brilliant company are what endures.
Stripping down “Cyrano de Bergerac” released that play’s energy; but playing a similar game here, its director delivers an uneven production more willful than wonderful.
This is a stylish, distinctive production.
Jamie Lloyd’s disrespectful vandalism is a conspiracy against the acting profession.
Anya Reiss’s brilliant adaptation of The Seagull gives Chekhov’s classic a contemporary edge and draws out the characters’ unrequited love for one another.
Unlike many of the fidgety teenagers clearly disappointed that their heroine remained fully clothed, I found this bare-bones production surprisingly persuasive.
Clarke’s dynamically expressive face lends itself to the stage and as such is a delight to watch, as are the other cast members.
Even if Jamie Lloyd's slow pacing is deliberate, it's mumbling misery.
The production is the least naturalistic, the least Chekhovian, I have seen.

cn.t: Lloyd's radical, stripped-back production divides critics. Clarke impresses in her West End debut, but the minimalist staging and slow pacing frustrate some while others find it gripping and contemporary.

vr.q: I gave this a 4 star review, I really enjoyed this production.
